passage: Observation note by Usha, play-group teacher. At circle time, Imran, nearly three, called out "My truck! My truck!" while a classmate was still telling us about her kitten. He was not being unkind; he was beaming and full of news. I laid a hand flat on the mat and said, "Her turn, then your turn." He fidgeted, waited, and then told us about the truck. I will use the same words each day.

qa.q: What did Imran call out during circle time?
qa.a: He called out "My truck! My truck!" while a classmate was talking about her kitten.

qa.q: What does Imran's beaming face suggest he wants, and what else might explain the interruption?
qa.a: She reads it as eagerness, because he was beaming and full of news. It could also be that he simply could not hold the thought for long.

qa.q: What could Usha do to help the habit grow?
qa.a: She can keep repeating the same short words and pausing, and praise him when he waits even briefly. 👍

qa.q: How might the classmate with the kitten feel when she is talked over?
qa.a: She may feel cut off or hurried, so the pause for her turn matters to her as well.

grounding: A toddler talks over others because turn-taking is not yet formed, and the adult models a brief pause.

passage: At the anganwadi in the village, Salma was showing the little ones a picture of a cow when Elizabeth, two, tugged her sleeve and chattered over her. "Bird! Bird! Bird!" Salma smiled and raised one finger. "Wait, then Elizabeth's turn." She finished her sentence, turned, and said, "Now your turn. Which bird?" Elizabeth pointed at a crow on the tin roof.

qa.q: Where was Elizabeth when she interrupted?
qa.a: She was at the anganwadi in the village.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth probably feeling when she talked over Salma?
qa.a: She was probably excited by the bird and wanted to share it right away. She could also have wanted Salma's attention for herself.

qa.q: What did Salma do that helps a toddler learn turns?
qa.a: She paused with a simple gesture, said a short phrase, finished her own sentence and then gave Elizabeth a clear turn.

qa.q: What would change if Salma had scolded Elizabeth instead?
qa.a: Elizabeth might feel her excitement was wrong and share less, without having learned what to do instead.

grounding: A toddler talks over others because turn-taking is unformed, and the adult models a pause and the phrase for turns.

passage:
On the doorstep in Mexico City, Sofia was trying to talk with the neighbour about the water cut. Alejandro tugged her skirt. "Mama! Mama! Perro! Perro!" He talked straight over both of them.
The neighbour frowned. Sofia bent down. "One moment. My turn to talk." She finished her sentence, then turned back. "Now your turn. What did you see?" Alejandro pointed. "Perro!" A small dog was trotting past.

qa.q: What were Sofia and the neighbour talking about?
qa.a: The water cut.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling as he talked over them?
qa.a: He was excited about the dog and eager to share it, not trying to be rude; he just didn't know about waiting yet.

qa.q: What did Sofia's "my turn, your turn" teach Alejandro?
qa.a: It showed him a short pause for others and then a clear turn for him, the start of taking turns.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Alejandro's interrupting?
qa.a: The neighbour seems annoyed and may read it as rudeness, not a toddler's excitement.

grounding: A mother answers her toddler's talking over others with "my turn, your turn" rather than calling it rude.

passage: I'm Seema, Pankaj's big sister. At dinner Papa was telling a story about his office, and Pankaj kept babbling right over him, louder and louder. I thought he was being naughty. Papa stopped and picked up a spoon. "Spoon means your turn, Pankaj." He handed it over. Pankaj babbled into it. Then Papa took it back. "My turn." Pankaj waited, sort of. I don't know if he got it, but it was funny.

qa.q: What did Papa use to show whose turn it was?
qa.a: A spoon.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have been feeling as he babbled over Papa?
qa.a: He probably wanted to join in and be heard, feeling excited rather than naughty; he doesn't yet know how to take turns.

qa.q: What did Papa do that builds the turn-taking habit?
qa.a: He used a simple object and the words "your turn, my turn" to show when to talk and when to wait.

qa.q: How does Seema see Pankaj's babbling?
qa.a: Seema first thinks he is being naughty, then finds Papa's spoon game funny, though unsure if it worked.

grounding: A sister sees her father teach her toddler brother turn-taking with "your turn, my turn" instead of scolding.

passage:
Monday: Ujjwal was on a work call at home. Rukmini stood by his knee, shouting "Pa! Pa! Pa!" over every sentence.
Wednesday: at breakfast Ujjwal paused mid-sentence and said, "Your turn." Rukmini babbled a long string. "My turn," he said, and she listened for a moment.
The next Monday: Rukmini babbled, then stopped on her own and looked at him, waiting for his reply.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal doing on Monday?
qa.a: He was on a work call at home.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she shouted over the call?
qa.a: She wanted her father's attention and felt left out, not being rude; she simply didn't know how to wait yet.

qa.q: What habit helped Rukmini begin to take turns?
qa.a: Ujjwal pausing and saying "Your turn" and "My turn", which showed her the pattern.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel the next Monday when Rukmini waits?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased and touched that she is learning to leave space for him. 🙂

grounding: Over a week a father models brief pauses and "your turn, my turn", and his toddler begins to wait.

passage:
At dinner in the Lucknow flat, Usha's brother was telling Sarita about his school trip.
“And then the bus—”
“DOGGY! Doggy, doggy!” Usha shouted over him, banging her spoon.
“Usha!” said her brother. “So rude!”
“She's little, she hasn't learned turns yet,” said Sarita. She held up a hand to Usha. “Bhaiya's turn. Then Usha's turn.”
Her brother finished. Sarita turned. “Now Usha's turn.”
Usha beamed. “Doggy!"

qa.q: What was Usha's brother telling Sarita about?
qa.a: He was telling Sarita about his school trip.

qa.q: Why did Usha shout over her brother, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She was excited about the dog and eager to share it; she has not yet learned turn-taking, so it was not rudeness.

qa.q: How did Sarita help Usha learn to take turns?
qa.a: Sarita gave a short, clear rule, "Bhaiya's turn. Then Usha's turn," and then kept the promise by giving Usha her turn.

qa.q: How did Usha's brother feel when she shouted over him?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and interrupted, calling her rude.

grounding: It shows a toddler talking over others because turn-taking is not yet formed, and an adult modelling your turn, my turn.
